subject: Blackwell fingerprints in six Chinese AI models
bodyMarkdown:
Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, and a report published on Thursday has changed what I will be reading it for. The claim in that report is that chips barred from export to China have been training China's strongest open models.

## What the weights appear to show

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher now running a shop called Unemployment Labs, published an analysis on Thursday saying he found Nvidia Blackwell fingerprints inside six Chinese open models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and V4-Pro, Moonshot's Kimi K3 and K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash. He works from **model weights**, the long lists of numbers a model learns during training and that these labs publish for anyone to download, matching their numerical quirks to specific hardware. The Decoder, which covered the report, put the two largest runs at roughly 4,500 Blackwell GPUs for Kimi K3 and about 3,000 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with something near 12,000 across five runs. I want to flag his own caution here. The report says the evidence supports, without proving, that Blackwell did the training, and rented capacity in a data centre outside China would leave the same traces.

## The fight it landed in

This dropped into an argument that was already loud in Washington. Axios reported on Wednesday that President Trump backed curbs on Nvidia's China sales three times while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled them, and NPR reported on Saturday that Commerce is under pressure for having cleared Chinese companies to handle Nvidia chips over national security objections. The line today is narrow. Blackwell cannot go to China, while the H200 can, under licences this administration granted. Beijing answered inside a day. Wire coverage of a Friday briefing quoted foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning saying China opposes the misuse of export controls and that such moves disrupt global industrial and supply chains. House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is a growing consensus in Congress for tightening the rules further.

## Why I am watching Tuesday

Nvidia's fiscal third quarter ended October 25, and MarketBeat puts consensus near $108.72 billion in revenue and $2.47 per share. My guess is that the revenue line will be the least interesting thing in the release. What I will read first is whatever the company says about China and about licensing, because that is where a policy change shows up long before it shows up in sales. There is a second-order problem underneath all of this. If something like 12,000 restricted GPUs really did end up training Chinese models, then export controls are a leakier instrument than either their defenders or their critics have been willing to say, and the sensible response to that is genuinely unclear. Tightening them raises the cost of a supply chain that Canadian investors are long whether they meant to be or not.

## The takeaway

Watch what Nvidia says about China on Tuesday after the close, not the headline revenue number. Treat the Blackwell claim as a strong hypothesis rather than a settled finding, since coverage of the report says the method has been reproduced on only one of the six models so far. If you hold a broad US index fund in an RRSP or TFSA, you already own a position in how this policy fight resolves, so it is worth knowing how big that position is. And when Ottawa eventually weighs in on chip rules, keep in mind that Canada buys compute rather than making it.
